title: Recognize possible trauma effects and prepare a suitable support route

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Possible trauma-related effects are not a diagnosis. A supportive peer can listen, offer ordinary practical help and assist access to qualified assessment, without requiring retelling or conducting exposure exercises.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: New fictional person: after a frightening event, Kai reports disturbed sleep and difficulty concentrating. Duration, medical history and other causes are unknown. Kai wants help locating a clinician but does not want to describe the event. Friend Jo is available ten minutes to find the existing clinic’s public booking route; no treatment or appointment is yet agreed.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Draft a response that respects disclosure choice and distinguishes possible explanation, assessment and practical help. Identify what would exceed Jo’s role.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A peer says “you seem calm, so trauma cannot be relevant” and asks for a detailed retelling to prove otherwise. What is wrong?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Acknowledge the difficulty and help with the requested route while keeping causes unknown. Later fiction: a request reaches the clinic; no assessment has occurred. Partial: kind words but pressure for details. Incorrect: diagnose PTSD from two symptoms or tell Kai to confront reminders alone. Current danger or rapidly worsening needs take priority over the exercise and a future appointment.
criteria: Possible effects are not converted to diagnosis
Peer help and professional assessment differ

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: Appearance does not settle cause or diagnosis, and disclosure is not a credibility test. Respect refusal, offer appropriate support and leave assessment to qualified care.
